IS6400 Week 3 Tutorial: Data Exploration¶

This tutorial follows the original "Week 3 - Description" notebook, but is aligned with the Week 3 assignment difficulty. It covers:

  • Data types (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio)
  • Percentiles and grouped descriptive statistics
  • Skewness and kurtosis
  • Visualization (histogram, boxplot, scatter, parallel coordinates)
  • Missing values: mean vs median vs KNN imputation
  • Outlier detection: IQR vs Z-score
  • Standardization: StandardScaler vs RobustScaler
  • Covariance, correlation, and correlation-vs-causation

How to use: Run each cell one by one (Shift+Enter). Read the markdown explanations carefully; the same techniques are required in the assignment.

1. Load the Iris Data¶

The Iris dataset contains 150 flowers from three species.
Each row is an object (record, sample, instance).
Each column is an attribute (variable, feature).

In [3]:

2. Descriptive Statistics, Percentiles, Skewness and Kurtosis¶

For each numeric attribute we report:

  • mean, median, mode
  • std, min, max
  • Q1, median, Q3, IQR
  • skewness (symmetry), kurtosis (tailedness)

Percentiles are important in real data: the 90th percentile of prices is often more meaningful than the mean.

In [5]:
def describe_col(df, col):
    s = df[col]
    q1, q3 = s.quantile(0.25), s.quantile(0.75)
    return pd.Series({
        'mean': s.mean(),
        'median': s.median(),
        'mode': s.mode().iloc[0],
        'std': s.std(),
        'min': s.min(),
        'max': s.max(),
        'Q1': q1,
        'Q3': q3,
        'range': s.max() - s.min(),
        'IQR': q3 - q1,
        'skew': s.skew(),
        'kurt': s.kurt()
    })

describe_col(data, 'sepal length')

Skewness near 0 → symmetric.
Positive skew → right tail longer than left tail.
Kurtosis near 0 → similar to normal distribution tails; large positive → heavy tails.

4. Data Visualization¶

4.1 Histogram¶

In [14]:
data['petal width'].hist(bins=20)
plt.title('Histogram of Petal Width')
plt.xlabel('Petal Width (cm)')

Multiple peaks suggest the variable may be a mixture of several populations (here, three species). This is an important warning about distributional shape.

plt.title('Boxplot of Iris Attributes')

Petal length and width have larger ranges than sepal width. No obvious extreme outliers — we will see what happens when we detect outliers with IQR and Z-score.

5. Missing Values: Mean vs Median vs KNN Imputation¶

Switch to a more realistic dataset: Airbnb.csv.
It contains missing values in review_scores_rating and bedrooms.

We compare three imputation methods and justify the preferred one.
This is exactly what the assignment requires.

In [28]:
cols = ['review_scores_rating', 'bedrooms']

# Mean
imp_mean = SimpleImputer(strategy='mean')
air[['review_scores_rating_mean', 'bedrooms_mean']] = imp_mean.fit_transform(air[cols])

# Median
imp_med = SimpleImputer(strategy='median')
air[['review_scores_rating_median', 'bedrooms_median']] = imp_med.fit_transform(air[cols])

# KNN
imp_knn = KNNImputer(n_neighbors=5)
knn_vals = imp_knn.fit_transform(air[cols])
air['review_scores_rating_knn'] = knn_vals[:, 0]
air['bedrooms_knn'] = knn_vals[:, 1]

def summary(col):
    s = air[col]
    return pd.Series({'mean': s.mean(), 'std': s.std(),
                      'min': s.min(), 'max': s.max(), 'skew': s.skew()})

pd.DataFrame({
    'review_mean': summary('review_scores_rating_mean'),
    'review_median': summary('review_scores_rating_median'),
    'review_knn': summary('review_scores_rating_knn'),
    'bed_mean': summary('bedrooms_mean'),
    'bed_median': summary('bedrooms_median'),
    'bed_knn': summary('bedrooms_knn'),
}).T
Out[28]:
mean std min max skew
review_mean 94.012789 6.898510 20.0 100.0 -3.777841
review_median 94.458309 6.948115 20.0 100.0 -3.884890
review_knn 94.095534 6.910205 20.0 100.0 -3.795248
bed_mean 1.271733 0.855334 0.0 10.0 2.005283
bed_median 1.271733 0.855334 0.0 10.0 2.005283
bed_knn 1.271733 0.855334 0.0 10.0 2.005283

Interpretation

  • review_scores_rating is left-skewed (values pile up near 100). Median imputation preserves this shape better than mean imputation.
  • bedrooms is right-skewed. KNN preserves the local structure, median is robust to outliers, mean is most sensitive.
  • Preferred choice: median for both — simple and robust. KNN is a valid alternative if local similarity matters.

We build air_clean with the preferred method.

In [30]:
air_clean = air.copy()
air_clean['review_scores_rating'] = air_clean['review_scores_rating_median']
air_clean['bedrooms'] = air_clean['bedrooms_median']

6. Outlier Detection: IQR vs Z-score¶

We apply two standard methods and compare their results.

In [32]:
def iqr_flag(s, k=1.5):
    q1, q3 = s.quantile(0.25), s.quantile(0.75)
    iqr = q3 - q1
    return (s < q1 - k * iqr) | (s > q3 + k * iqr)

def z_flag(s, threshold=3):
    z = (s - s.mean()) / s.std()
    return z.abs() > threshold

for col in ['log_price', 'accommodates', 'bathrooms']:
    n_iqr = iqr_flag(air_clean[col]).sum()
    n_z = z_flag(air_clean[col]).sum()
    print(f"{col}: IQR -> {n_iqr}, Z-score -> {n_z}")

log_price: IQR -> 1453, Z-score -> 453
accommodates: IQR -> 3299, Z-score -> 1378
bathrooms: IQR -> 14307, Z-score -> 1878
In [33]:
air_clean['outlier_iqr'] = iqr_flag(air_clean['log_price'])
air_clean['outlier_iqr'].mean().round(4)
Out[33]:
0.0213

Insight: IQR usually flags more points because it does not assume a normal distribution. Z-score assumes an approximately Gaussian variable, so it can miss heavy-tail outliers and over-flag variables that are not normal.

7. Standardization: StandardScaler vs RobustScaler¶

Different attributes have different scales.

  • StandardScaler: subtract mean, divide by std. Sensitive to outliers.
  • RobustScaler: subtract median, divide by IQR. Robust to outliers.
In [36]:
feats = ['accommodates', 'bathrooms', 'bedrooms', 'beds', 'review_scores_rating']
X = air_clean[feats].copy()

X_std = pd.DataFrame(StandardScaler().fit_transform(X), columns=[f + '_std' for f in feats])
X_rob = pd.DataFrame(RobustScaler().fit_transform(X), columns=[f + '_rob' for f in feats])

print("StandardScaler:")
print(X_std.describe().T[['mean', 'std', 'min', 'max']])
print()
print("RobustScaler:")
print(X_rob.describe().T[['mean', 'std', 'min', 'max']])

StandardScaler:

accommodates_std          3.477992e-17  1.000007  -1.004790   6.021728
bathrooms_std             7.612995e-18  1.000007  -2.185948  12.029751
bedrooms_std             -6.924697e-17  1.000007  -1.486837  10.204586
beds_std                 -8.895733e-17  1.000007  -1.381144  13.212629
review_scores_rating_std -9.453150e-16  1.000007 -10.716411   0.797588

bathrooms_rob             0.230160  0.562762  -1.000000   7.000000
bedrooms_rob              0.271733  0.855334  -1.000000   9.000000
beds_rob                  0.703506  1.233412  -1.000000  17.000000
review_scores_rating_rob -0.256948  1.158019 -12.666667   0.666667

When to use which:

  • Use StandardScaler when features are roughly symmetric and outliers are rare.
  • Use RobustScaler when features have outliers or skewed distributions.

8. Covariance, Correlation, and Correlation ≠ Causation¶

Covariance measures joint variation but depends on scale.
Correlation is scale-free, in [-1, +1], and measures only linear association.

In [39]:
corr_cols = ['log_price', 'accommodates', 'bathrooms', 'bedrooms',
             'beds', 'number_of_reviews', 'review_scores_rating']

cov_matrix = air_clean[corr_cols].cov()
corr_matrix = air_clean[corr_cols].corr()

print("Correlation matrix:")
corr_matrix.round(3)

Correlation matrix:

air_clean[corr_cols].corr()['log_price'].drop('log_price').sort_values(key=abs, ascending=False).head(5)
Out[41]:
accommodates            0.578068
bedrooms                0.482682
beds                    0.469700
bathrooms               0.376758
review_scores_rating    0.080912
Name: log_price, dtype: float64

Correlation ≠ Causation. A larger accommodates is strongly correlated with a higher log_price, but size does not cause price by itself. Location, amenities, and demand are confounding factors that affect both.

This is exactly the kind of reasoning required in the assignment.

  • Attribute type table for every column: nominal / ordinal / interval / ratio; discrete / continuous; symmetric or asymmetric binary. Include one short reason per column.
  • Full descriptive statistics for every numerical variable: mean, median, mode, std, min, max, Q1, Q3, IQR, skewness, kurtosis.

1.2 Descriptive Statistics for Numerical Variables¶

The following table reports the central tendency, dispersion, range and distributional shape of each meaningful numerical variable. The listing ID was excluded because it is an identifier rather than a quantitative measurement. Missing values were retained at this stage, and each statistic was calculated using the available observations.

In [50]:
numeric_cols = [
    "log_price",
    "accommodates",
    "bathrooms",
    "number_of_reviews",
    "review_scores_rating",
    "bedrooms",
    "beds"
]

def descriptive_statistics(df, columns):
    results = []

    for col in columns:
        # Drop missing values only for calculating this variable's statistics
        s = df[col].dropna()

        q1 = s.quantile(0.25)
        q3 = s.quantile(0.75)

        results.append({
            "Variable": col,
            "Valid N": s.count(),
            "Missing": df[col].isna().sum(),
            "Mean": s.mean(),
            "Median": s.median(),
            "Mode": s.mode().iloc[0],
            "Std": s.std(),
            "Min": s.min(),
            "Max": s.max(),
            "Q1": q1,
            "Q3": q3,
            "IQR": q3 - q1,
            "Skewness": s.skew(),
            "Kurtosis": s.kurt()
        })

    return pd.DataFrame(results).set_index("Variable")

The numerical variables show several substantially non-normal distributions. The mean log price was 4.775, slightly above its median of 4.700, while its skewness of 0.526 indicated only moderate right skewness. This suggests that the logarithmic transformation reduced, but did not completely eliminate, the long right tail normally found in accommodation prices.

The count variables were considerably more skewed. The mean number of reviews was 20.830, whereas the median was only 6 and the mode was 0. Its skewness of 3.632 and maximum of 532 indicate that a relatively small number of listings received exceptionally many reviews. Similarly, accommodates and beds had positive skewness values of 2.178 and 3.238 respectively.

Review scores exhibited the opposite pattern. Their mean was 94.013, median was 96, and mode was 100, producing a strong negative skewness of -3.328. Most observed ratings were therefore concentrated near the upper end of the scale, with a relatively small number of low ratings forming a long left tail. In addition, bathrooms and bedrooms both had an IQR of zero because the middle 50% of observations were equal to one. This concentration should be considered when applying IQR-based outlier detection later.

The categorical distributions reveal considerable imbalance in several attributes. Apartments accounted for 48,772 listings, or 71.58% of the sample, while houses accounted for a further 24.12%. Townhouses and lofts together represented only 4.30%, so conclusions concerning these less common property types should be interpreted more cautiously.

The imbalance was even stronger for bed type: 97.24% of listings offered a real bed. Strict was the most common cancellation policy at 43.74%, followed by flexible at 30.51% and moderate at 25.59%. The two super-strict categories were extremely rare, particularly super_strict_60, which contained only eight observations.

The dataset was also geographically concentrated. NYC represented 45.84% of all listings and LA represented 29.26%, meaning that 75.10% of the sample came from these two cities. In addition, 73.59% of listings charged a cleaning fee. Almost all hosts had a profile picture (99.43%), whereas 67.36% had verified their identity. Both host-related variables contained 180 missing values, equivalent to 0.26% of the full sample.

1.4 Percentile Analysis of Log Price and Original Price¶

The original price scale was recovered by exponentiating log_price. The 25th, 50th, 75th, 90th, 95th and 99th percentiles were calculated independently on both scales. The independently calculated price percentiles were also compared with the exponentiated log-price percentiles.

In [56]:
# Recover price on its original scale
air["price"] = np.exp(air["log_price"])

percentile_levels = [0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99]

log_percentiles = air["log_price"].quantile(percentile_levels)
price_percentiles = air["price"].quantile(percentile_levels)
exp_log_percentiles = np.exp(log_percentiles)

percentile_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Log-price percentile": log_percentiles,
    "Price percentile": price_percentiles,
    "Exp(log-price percentile)": exp_log_percentiles
})

percentile_table["Difference"] = (
    percentile_table["Price percentile"]
    - percentile_table["Exp(log-price percentile)"]
)

percentile_table.index = [
    "25th", "50th", "75th", "90th", "95th", "99th"
]

display(
    percentile_table.round({
        "Log-price percentile": 4,
        "Price percentile": 2,
        "Exp(log-price percentile)": 2,
        "Difference": 6
    })
)

print(
    "Do the two calculation methods agree?",
    np.allclose(price_percentiles, exp_log_percentiles)
)
Log-price percentile Price percentile Exp(log-price percentile) Difference
25th 4.2905 73.0 73.0 0.0
50th 4.7005 110.0 110.0 0.0
75th 5.1930 180.0 180.0 0.0
90th 5.7004 299.0 299.0 0.0
95th 6.0210 412.0 412.0 0.0
99th 6.8565 950.0 950.0 0.0 
Do the two calculation methods agree? True

The median log price was 4.7005, corresponding to a median price of 110 on the original scale. The 25th and 75th price percentiles were 73 and 180 respectively. At the upper end, the 90th, 95th and 99th percentiles were 299, 412 and 950. The 99th-percentile price was therefore approximately 8.64 times the median, demonstrating the long upper tail of the original price distribution.

The exponential function is strictly increasing, so it preserves the rank order of observations. Under a population-quantile or order-statistic definition, this implies that $Q_p(exp(X)) = exp(Q_p(X))$. However, sample quantile software may interpolate between adjacent observations. Because linear interpolation and a nonlinear exponential transformation do not generally commute, small numerical differences can arise when quantiles are calculated independently on the two scales.

In this dataset, the independently calculated price percentiles were equal to the exponentiated log-price percentiles at all six requested levels. This occurred because the relevant percentile positions corresponded to identical or repeated observed price values. Therefore, the transformation relationship should be verified empirically rather than assumed to be different in every dataset.

1.5 Grouped Comparison of Log Price¶

Log price was compared across cities and property types using the mean, median, standard deviation and interquartile range. The median represents the price of a typical listing and is less sensitive to extreme values, whereas the standard deviation and IQR provide complementary measures of variability. Group sample sizes were also reported because the categorical variables were not evenly represented.

In [59]:
def grouped_log_price_statistics(df, group_column):
    grouped = df.groupby(group_column)["log_price"]

    result = grouped.agg(
        Count="count",
        Mean="mean",
        Median="median",
        Std="std",
        Q1=lambda x: x.quantile(0.25),
        Q3=lambda x: x.quantile(0.75)
    )

    result["IQR"] = result["Q3"] - result["Q1"]

    # Display groups from the highest to the lowest median
    return result.sort_values("Median", ascending=False)

property_statistics = grouped_log_price_statistics(air, "property_type")

San Francisco had the highest median log price at 5.0752, corresponding to a median price of approximately 160 on the original scale. Chicago had the lowest median log price at 4.5951, corresponding to approximately 99. The typical listing price in San Francisco was therefore about 61 units higher than that in Chicago.

DC showed the greatest city-level variability. Its standard deviation of 0.8160 and IQR of 0.9734 were both the largest among the six cities. Because both the outlier-sensitive standard deviation and the robust IQR produced the same conclusion, the evidence that DC had the most dispersed log-price distribution is relatively strong.

Among property types, lofts had the highest median log price at 4.9767, corresponding to a median original-scale price of approximately 145. Houses showed the greatest variability, with a standard deviation of 0.8766 and an IQR of 1.1727. The mean log price for houses was 4.7982, considerably above the median of 4.6052, suggesting that relatively expensive houses produced a right-tailed distribution.

1.6 Key Insights¶

  1. Log transformation substantially reduced price skewness. The mean log price was 4.775 and the median was 4.700, while the skewness was only 0.526. The relatively small difference between the mean and median suggests that log_price was considerably more balanced than a typical raw-price distribution, although some right skewness remained.

  2. The original price distribution still had a pronounced upper tail. The median price was 110, while the 90th, 95th and 99th percentiles were 299, 412 and 950 respectively. The 99th-percentile price was approximately 8.64 times the median, indicating a small but economically important group of very expensive listings.

  3. Most listings received relatively few reviews, but a small number were exceptionally popular. The median number of reviews was only 6 and the mode was 0, compared with a mean of 20.830 and a maximum of 532. The resulting skewness of 3.632 confirms a strong right-tailed distribution.

  4. Review ratings were concentrated close to the upper boundary. The mean rating was 94.013, the median was 96 and the mode was 100. Its skewness of -3.328 indicates that most observed ratings were high, with a relatively small number of low ratings forming a long left tail.

  5. The dataset was dominated by a small number of listing categories. Apartments represented 71.58% of all listings, while houses represented 24.12%. Together, these two categories accounted for 95.70% of the sample. Similarly, 97.24% of listings offered a real bed, leaving very limited representation for alternative bed types.

  6. The sample was geographically concentrated and did not represent the six cities equally. NYC accounted for 45.84% of listings and LA accounted for 29.26%, meaning that 75.10% of the entire dataset came from these two cities. Consequently, aggregate statistics are likely to be influenced heavily by the NYC and LA markets.

  7. San Francisco had the highest typical price, whereas DC had the greatest price dispersion. SF's median log price was 5.0752, equivalent to a median original-scale price of approximately 160, compared with about 99 in Chicago. DC had both the largest standard deviation (0.8160) and the largest IQR (0.9734), showing the greatest within-city variability.

  8. Lofts were the most expensive typical property type, but houses were the most heterogeneous. Lofts had the highest median log price at 4.9767, equivalent to an original-scale median of approximately 145. Houses had the highest standard deviation of 0.8766 and the highest IQR of 1.1727, indicating the widest range of price levels among property types.

Mean, median and KNN imputation produced similar but not identical rating distributions. Mean imputation preserved the overall mean at 94.0128 but reduced the standard deviation from 7.8319 among observed ratings to 6.8985. This occurred because all missing values were replaced by the same central value, artificially concentrating the distribution.

Median imputation produced a mean of 94.4583, a standard deviation of 6.9481 and skewness of -3.8849. KNN imputation produced corresponding values of 94.4006, 6.9418 and -3.8709. Median imputation was selected because the rating distribution was strongly left-skewed and bounded at 100, making the median less sensitive to the relatively small number of very low ratings. It was also more transparent than KNN, whose similarity calculation was largely based on bedroom count in this comparison.

The bedroom variable contained no missing values. Consequently, all three methods left its mean, standard deviation and skewness unchanged at 1.2717, 0.8553 and 2.0053 respectively.

In [134]:
def iqr_flag(series, multiplier=1.5):

    q1 = series.quantile(0.25)
    q3 = series.quantile(0.75)

    iqr = q3 - q1

    lower = q1 - multiplier * iqr
    upper = q3 + multiplier * iqr

    flags = (
        (series < lower) |
        (series > upper)
    )

    return flags, lower, upper

def zscore_flag(series, threshold=3):

    z = (
        (series - series.mean()) /
        series.std()
    )

    return z.abs() > threshold
    
outlier_rows = []

for col in [
    "log_price",
    "accommodates",
    "bathrooms"
]:

    iqr_flags, lower, upper = iqr_flag(
        air_clean[col]
    )

    z_flags = zscore_flag(
        air_clean[col]
    )

    outlier_rows.append({
        "Variable": col,
        "Method": "IQR",
        "Outlier count": int(iqr_flags.sum()),
        "Percentage (%)": iqr_flags.mean() * 100,
        "Lower bound": lower,
        "Upper bound": upper
    })

    outlier_rows.append({
        "Variable": col,
        "Method": "Z-score",
        "Outlier count": int(z_flags.sum()),
        "Percentage (%)": z_flags.mean() * 100,
        "Lower bound": np.nan,

The IQR method identified more outliers than the Z-score method for all three variables. For log price, IQR flagged 1,453 observations (2.13%), whereas Z-score flagged 453 observations (0.66%). For accommodation capacity, the corresponding counts were 3,299 (4.84%) and 1,378 (2.02%).

The largest disagreement occurred for bathrooms. The first and third quartiles were both equal to one, resulting in an IQR of zero. Consequently, the IQR rule classified every value other than one bathroom as an outlier, producing 14,307 flagged observations (21.00%). Many of these observations are likely to be legitimate multi-bathroom or half-bathroom properties rather than data errors.

The comparison demonstrates that statistical outlier rules should not be used as automatic deletion rules, particularly for discrete and highly concentrated variables. All observations were retained, and an outlier_iqr Boolean column was added to identify the 1,453 log-price observations flagged by the IQR rule.

accommodates 0.0 0.0 1.0 1.0
bathrooms 0.0 0.0 0.0 0.0

beds 0.0 0.0 1.0 1.0
review_scores_rating 0.0 -0.5 0.5 1.0

StandardScaler produced means close to zero and standard deviations close to one for all five features. However, extreme standardized values remained. For example, the minimum standardised review score was -10.7164, while the maximum standardised number of beds was 13.2126. This demonstrates that standardisation changes the measurement scale but does not remove outliers.

RobustScaler did not produce zero means or unit standard deviations because it centres each variable using the median and scales it using the IQR. It is therefore preferable when variables are skewed or contain extreme values. This is relevant to the Airbnb data because the capacity variables are right-skewed and review ratings are strongly left-skewed.

Bathrooms and bedrooms require additional caution because both had an IQR of zero. In these cases, RobustScaler avoided division by zero by using a unit scale, so the transformation primarily subtracted the median rather than performing full IQR scaling. Overall, RobustScaler is more resistant to outliers, whereas StandardScaler is preferable when distributions are approximately symmetric and extreme observations are rare.

The three features most strongly correlated with log price were accommodates (0.5781), bedrooms (0.4827), and beds (0.4697). All three describe listing capacity, indicating that larger listings tend to have higher prices. However, these predictors also contained overlapping information. For example, the correlation between accommodates and beds was 0.8290, while bedrooms and beds had a correlation of 0.7298.

The positive correlation between accommodates and log price does not establish that increasing the stated accommodation capacity would cause the price to rise. Property size is a concrete confounding variable: larger properties can accommodate more guests and also command higher prices. City, neighbourhood and property type may create similar confounding relationships.

Because the dataset is observational and cross-sectional, the analysis can identify associations but cannot establish a causal effect. A causal conclusion would require stronger assumptions, additional control variables, or an appropriate causal identification design.

The project dataset contains 10,000 complete student records, so no missing-value imputation is required. Current grade averaged 78.75 with a standard deviation of 9.40, while mean attendance and assessment-completion rates were 0.888 and 0.792. Both behaviours were positively related to achievement, but assessment completion had the stronger relationship: its correlation with current grade was 0.593, compared with 0.440 for attendance. Attendance and assessment completion were also moderately correlated at 0.451, suggesting overlapping engagement information.

For later modelling, current grade can be treated as a continuous target, with attendance and assessment completion as interpretable predictors. Their joint use may improve prediction, although multicollinearity should be checked. Nonlinear effects may also matter because improvement from very low to moderate engagement may differ from improvement near full engagement. These observational relationships are not necessarily causal: prior attainment, programme difficulty, wellbeing and access to support may influence both engagement and grades. A later model should therefore include appropriate controls, examine nonlinear terms, and be evaluated on a held-out test set or through cross-validation.

Submission Checklist¶

  • ipynb file with all cells executed.
  • Exported HTML file.
  • All plots have titles, axis labels, and interpretations.
  • All code is reproducible.
  • The submission is well-structured and easy to follow.
